info.headline: Build correct sentences and short, scaffolded paragraphs with frames and word banks
info.summary: Level A writers move from single words to one complete, correct sentence and then to a few connected sentences. Every task supplies a sentence frame, a labeled word bank, and a model so students can succeed before writing independently. The focus is producing accurate, purposeful sentences across descriptive, informational, opinion, and narrative purposes.
info.distinguishes: Level A output is at the sentence to short-paragraph level (typically 1-4 sentences, roughly 10-40 words). Heavy scaffolding is always present: cloze blanks, sentence frames, picture/word banks, and ordering or sorting tasks that build paragraph awareness before composition. Students rely on a provided model and finish frames before attempting independence. Vocabulary is everyday plus a few academic anchor words.
canDo: I can write one complete sentence with a capital letter and an end mark.
I can use a sentence frame and a word bank to describe a picture or place.
I can finish a reason sentence using the word because.
I can put short sentences in time order to make a small paragraph.
I can sort sentences into topic, detail, and closing parts.
I can write a short opinion sentence with one reason.
focusAreas: sentence frames and labeled word banks

activities.title: My Opinion: A Meal I Love
activities.skill: Writing an opinion sentence with a reason

activities.directions: Write one or two sentences that tell your opinion about a meal you like. Use the word 'because' to give one reason. Use the frames to help you.
activities.prompt: What is a meal you love to eat? Tell your opinion and give one reason why you love it.
writeFor: A clear opinion (what meal you like)
The word 'because' followed by a reason
A capital letter at the start and a period at the end
vocabulary: what you think or feel about something
opinión: lo que piensas o sientes sobre algo
why you think or feel that way
razón: por qué piensas o sientes así
the one you like the most
favorito: el que más te gusta
activities.correct: A strong answer states an opinion and gives one reason joined by 'because', for example: 'My favorite meal is rice and beans. I love it because it tastes warm and reminds me of home.'
activities.hint: Start by naming the meal. Then write 'because' and tell one reason your body or your heart likes it.
activities.support: Choose your meal from the word bank, fill the first frame, then say 'because' out loud and finish the sentence.
activities.extension: Add a second reason using the word 'also', for example: 'I also love it because it is easy to share.'

info.headline: Compose cohesive paragraphs with claims, evidence, and academic transitions
info.summary: Level B writers compose multi-sentence paragraphs that organize a claim, evidence, and a conclusion. Frames and models are still available but used as a starting point toward independence; students revise for precision and connect ideas with academic transitions. The focus is developing coherent descriptive, informational, opinion/argument, and narrative paragraphs for a purpose and audience.
info.distinguishes: Level B output is at the full-paragraph level (typically 4-7 sentences, roughly 50-120 words) rather than single sentences. Scaffolds shift from fill-in cloze toward optional frames, revision prompts, and self-checks; students write independently and then refine. Tasks add audience awareness, counterclaims, comparison/contrast, sensory and figurative language, and cohesive transitions. Vocabulary includes precise academic and content-area terms.
canDo: I can write a paragraph with a claim, evidence, and a concluding sentence.
I can use academic transitions to connect my ideas (for example, however, as a result).
I can revise a weak sentence into a stronger, more precise one.
I can compare two choices in writing using contrast transitions.
I can address the other side of an argument with a counterclaim.
I can write a descriptive or narrative paragraph with sensory details and time order.

C.teacherSummary: Built for grades 6-8 multilingual learners near exit (about 4.0-4.5). Many are long-term ELs whose writing lags their reading, so tasks focus on the moves that separate a 4 from an exit score: reasoning that explains evidence, precise academic vocabulary, cohesive transitions, and complex sentences. Constructed tasks include three sample answers (A, B, C) that show growth.

info.headline: Write like an expert: claim, evidence, reasoning, and polished academic sentences.
info.summary: Level C writers compose argument and explanatory paragraphs that use specific evidence, explain their reasoning, and address counterclaims. They revise their own and others' writing for precise vocabulary, logical transitions, and complex sentences that combine ideas. Constructed tasks come with three sample answers so students can see exactly how a paragraph grows from simple to fully developed, and printable planners support longer essays.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level B, Level C writing is expected to be cohesive across a full paragraph or more (roughly 100-180 words), to use evidence such as data or quotations, and to explain reasoning rather than just list reasons. Revision tasks target precision (replacing vague words), sentence combining with although, which, and because, and transitions that show exact relationships (consequently, nevertheless, for instance).

chart.title: Average Bean Plant Height After 3 Weeks

models.A: Light makes plants grow. The plant with 12 hours is 24. The plant with 0 hours is 4. Plants need light.
models.B: More light makes bean plants grow taller. According to the graph, plants with 12 hours of light grew 24 centimeters. Plants with no light grew only 4 centimeters. This happens because plants use light to make food. So light is important for plants.
models.C: The data shows that the more light bean plants receive, the taller they grow. According to the graph, plants that received 12 hours of light a day reached an average of 24 centimeters, while plants kept in darkness grew only 4 centimeters. Even 4 hours of light nearly tripled growth compared to no light. This pattern makes sense because plants use light energy for photosynthesis, the process that produces the sugar they need to build new cells. As a result, plants with more light can make more food and grow more. Therefore, light is a key factor in how tall bean plants grow.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Northern Hemisphere has summer in June and winter in December. Use the diagram and precise science vocabulary.

picture.alt: A diagram of the Sun in the center with Earth shown at two places in its orbit. On the left, Earth's tilted axis leans its northern half toward the Sun, and sunlight hits the north directly. On the right, on the opposite side of the orbit, the same tilt now leans the northern half away from the Sun, and sunlight hits the north at a low slant.

models.A: Earth goes around the Sun. Earth is tilted. In summer it is close. In winter it is far.
models.B: We have seasons because Earth is tilted. In June, the top of Earth leans toward the Sun, so it gets more sunlight and it is summer. In December, the top of Earth leans away from the Sun, so it gets less sunlight and it is winter. The tilt stays the same all year.
models.C: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer. As a result, the ground and air absorb more energy, and it is summer. Six months later, in December, Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, and the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. Sunlight hits it at a low angle and spreads out, and days are shorter, so it is winter. Many people think seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun, but it is actually the tilt that matters.

activities.correct: Paragraph saved. A strong explanation names the tilt as the cause, explains June and December with cause-effect language, and uses precise words like axis, orbit, and direct sunlight.
activities.hint: Distance is NOT the reason for seasons. Focus on the tilt: which half leans toward the Sun in each month?
activities.support: Explanatory structure: topic sentence (the cause) → June (what and why) → December (what and why) → conclusion.

activities.directions: Read the claim and the evidence. Write a paragraph (5-7 sentences) that states the claim, gives evidence, presents a counterclaim fairly, and rebuts it.
activities.prompt: Claim: Middle schools should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Evidence you may use: teens' sleep cycles shift so most cannot fall asleep before 11 p.m.; schools that started later saw better attendance. Write your paragraph with a counterclaim and rebuttal.
activities.responsePlaceholder: Middle schools should ___. Research shows ___. Some people argue that ___. However, ___.
writeFor: the claim
evidence with a source or fact

models.A: School should start late. Kids are tired. Some people say no. But sleep is important.
models.B: Middle schools should start at 8:30 or later. Research shows that teenagers cannot fall asleep before 11 p.m. Schools that start later have better attendance. Some people argue that a later start is hard for working parents. However, students need sleep to learn. Therefore, schools should start later.
models.C: Middle schools should start at 8:30 a.m. or later so that students can get the sleep they need. Research shows that teenagers' sleep cycles shift during puberty, so most cannot fall asleep before 11 p.m., and schools that moved to later start times saw better attendance. Some people argue that a later start creates problems for working parents who leave home early. Admittedly, this is a real concern for many families. Nevertheless, schools could solve it by opening the building early with supervised breakfast and study time, so students have a safe place to be. Therefore, a later start would protect students' health without leaving families behind.

activities.title: Worksheet — Revision Workshop: Transitions, Words, Sentences
activities.skill: Revising a paragraph for cohesion, precision, and sentence variety
activities.directions: Revise the weak draft paragraph step by step. Then rewrite the whole paragraph in its best form.

sheet.heading: Part I — Read the draft
items: Draft: "Recycling is good. It helps a lot. People throw away stuff. The stuff goes to landfills. Landfills are getting full. We should recycle more. It is a good thing to do."

sheet.heading: Part II — Precise words
items: Replace "helps a lot" with a specific benefit: ______________

sheet.heading: Part III — Combine sentences
items: Combine sentences 3-5 into ONE complex sentence using because, which, or so: ______________________________

sheet.heading: Part IV — Add transitions
items: Add a transition that shows a result (as a result, consequently): ______________
Add a transition that shows a conclusion (therefore, for these reasons): ______________

sheet.heading: Part V — Rewrite
items: Rewrite the full paragraph with your revisions (5-6 sentences): ______________________________
☐ No vague words (good, stuff, a lot).  ☐ At least one complex sentence.  ☐ At least two transitions.

answerKey: Part II (sample): good → beneficial or essential; helps a lot → reduces waste and saves natural resources; stuff → plastic bottles, paper, and cans.
Part III (sample): People throw away plastic, paper, and cans, which end up in landfills that are quickly filling up.
Part IV (sample): As a result, ...; Therefore, ...

Part V (sample): Recycling is essential for our community. When people throw away plastic bottles, paper, and cans, these materials end up in landfills, which are quickly running out of space. As a result, cities must find new land for trash. Recycling reduces this waste and saves natural resources like trees and oil. Therefore, our school should make recycling bins available in every classroom.
